slides.title: Principle and purpose
bullets: Aminotransferases (ALT and AST) are enzymes that carry amino groups between molecules; ALT is found in the cytoplasm of liver, kidney, myocardial and pancreatic cells.
L-alanine and α-ketoglutarate are turned by ALT into pyruvate and L-glutamate.
Pyruvate, with LDH, oxidises NADH to L-lactate; the loss of NADH is followed as a fall in absorbance at 340 nm.
The rate of change of absorbance per minute is proportional to ALT activity.
It is used in the diagnosis of liver disease.

slides.title: Specimen and reagents
bullets: Specimen: non-haemolysed serum; EDTA or heparin plasma.
R1 — Tris buffer and L-alanine; R2 — LDH and NADH; R3 — α-ketoglutarate.
Working reagent: dissolve the contents of the R2 vial carefully in the matching volume of R1 buffer.
Stability of the working reagent: 30 days at 2–8 °C; 24 hours at room temperature.
The volumes, times and concentrations given belong to the kit named in the manual (Hospitex Diagnostics); with another kit follow its instructions.

slides.title: Procedure (manual)
bullets: 1. Put into the cuvette 0.5 mL (1 mL) of working reagent and 50 µL (100 µL) of sample.
2. Mix and incubate for 3 minutes at 37 °C.
3. Then add 50 µL (100 µL) of R3 to the cuvette.
4. Mix and, after 1 minute of incubation at 37 °C, measure the rate of change of absorbance (ΔA/min).

slides.title: Procedure (manual)
bullets: 5. Measuring conditions: wavelength 340 nm, 37 °C, 1 cm cuvette, zero — distilled water or air.
6. Volumes in brackets are for a standard cuvette.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: ALT (U/L) = ΔA/min × 1905 (at 340 nm); at 366 nm ΔA/min × 3543.
The manual also gives an alternative: R3 is added to the working reagent 10:1 to make a monoreagent (5 days at 2–8 °C), for which the factor is 1746.
Linearity up to 300 U/L; at very high activity the sample is diluted 1:4 or 1:9 with saline and the result multiplied by 5 or 10.
Reference in the manual: up to 40 U/L; each laboratory is advised to adjust the reference range itself.

ALT rises: early in acute (including viral) hepatitis, before jaundice appears; in liver-cell necrosis, severe muscle trauma, myositis, myocarditis; relatively in paroxysmal tachycardia and hypertensive crisis.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Deviations in temperature (37 °C) and incubation time directly affect the kinetic measurement.
If the working reagent is out of date or was stored wrongly (outside 2–8 °C), NADH breaks down and the result is distorted.
Do not test haemolysed, turbid or lipaemic samples.
The manual says ALT can also be determined with a calibrator of known enzyme activity, and that accuracy must be checked with control sera.
Quality control: measure a control serum in every analytical series and record the result on the control chart.

slides.title: Method not included
bullets: The Aripova book also describes a colorimetric determination of ALT with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (DNPH) (normal 0.1–0.68 mmol/L).
This older colorimetric method is not included in the protocol: the kinetic method matches the current kits recommended in the manual and is more accurate.
The reference values of the two methods differ in units and method and must not be compared.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Working reagent: dissolve the contents of the R2 vial in the matching volume of R1 buffer; stable for 30 days at 2–8 °C and 24 hours at room temperature.
Monoreagent for the analyser: R3 (α-ketoglutarate) is added to the working reagent at a 10:1 ratio; it keeps for 5 days at 2–8 °C and is warmed to 37 °C before use.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Calibration: by factor (K) — 1746 with the monoreagent; or calibrate with a calibrator of known activity, and the accuracy must be checked with control sera.
Zero: against distilled water or air; measure at 340 nm, 37 °C, 1 cm cuvette.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The values belong to the Hospitex Diagnostics kit and the Screen Master Plus photometer in the manual. The IFU of the kit you use and the analyser manual always take precedence — check the parameters against them.

slides.title: Semi-automatic analyser: ALT programme
rows: Inconsistent in the source: 5.0 µL in the programme, 50 µL manually — take it from the IFU

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Serum and plasma are potentially infectious: wear gloves; never pipette by mouth.
When handling kit reagents follow the warnings in the instructions.
Used cuvettes and tubes are disinfected.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used in routine screening of liver health and to help diagnose or monitor liver problems, usually as part of a liver function panel. Some liver diseases raise ALT before symptoms appear, so the test may help detect them early.

Ordered when there are symptoms of liver damage (for example jaundice, dark urine or light-colored stool, abdominal swelling or pain, frequent itching) or a high risk of liver damage: family history of liver disease, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, or hepatitis or exposure to it.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: ALT is usually measured together with AST in a liver function panel. Because ALT is found mostly in the liver, it checks more specifically for liver damage.
Physiology: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, and its blood level is usually low. When liver cells are damaged, they release ALT into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
cols: Possible causes of liver damage with a high ALT: hepatitis, infection, cirrhosis, liver cancer, other liver diseases, a lack of blood flow to the liver, certain medicines (such as cholesterol or pain medicines) and poisons.
Low ALT is not common and may lead to further testing. Possible causes include vitamin B6 deficiency and chronic kidney disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
cols: Cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern: ALT and AST are raised disproportionately to alkaline phosphatase. It points to liver-cell injury; the work-up looks for viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, medicines and other causes.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALT is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: A high ALT does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Age, sex, weight, certain medicines and dietary supplements, intense exercise and the phase of the menstrual cycle can affect the result.
Limitations: ALT is interpreted together with the other liver tests. It may help tell acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not reflect how much of the liver is damaged.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

The liver’s synthetic function (hepatocellular failure pattern) is judged not by enzymes but by proteins the liver makes: albumin and prothrombin time (PT/INR); bilirubin also reflects the liver’s clearing work. A high ALT by itself does not mean liver failure.
